paragraphs.tag: MAP: hook-1 | LOCKED HOOK. Frame 0: North Korea, Nov 1950, NIGHT look (option 1): red UN columns strung out on the valley roads north of the Chongchon, flags (US 48-star, ROK, UN); blue counters in the mountains around them already sliding forward. 0.3 s: BIG card slams (hit + shake) and ticks 0 -> 300,000 CHINESE SOLDIERS (ticks); red recon planes (c47g, red) sweep over, the blue counters freeze and fade to ghost outlines under snow; stamp NEVER SEEN (hit + shake); camera DIVE (zoom whoosh) onto the Chongchon valley; red caption card "END THE WAR" (MacArthur, 24 NOV)
paragraphs.text: Three hundred thousand Chinese soldiers. Marched into North Korea in secret, and not one unit was spotted from the air. And the Americans walking into those mountains believed the war was almost over.

paragraphs.tag: MAP: hook-2 | Beat every 2-4 s: NIGHT 25 NOV: the mountains light up, blue counters appear everywhere at once (hit), bugle-call caption, MG fire + impacts on the red columns (shake); white-flash cut -> DECEMBER 1950: zoom-out whoosh to all of Korea: red arrows stream south past Pyongyang (city ring flips blue, stamp ABANDONED) to the 38th parallel (line glows); stamp OUT OF NORTH KOREA (hit + shake); small caption "LONGEST RETREAT IN US MILITARY HISTORY" - EIGHTH ARMY HISTORY
paragraphs.text: On the night of the twenty-fifth of November, the mountains came alive. Within a month, the US Eighth Army had been driven out of North Korea, in what the US Army itself calls the longest retreat in its history.

paragraphs.tag: MAP: hook-3 | Twist as action, hard cut, dark: mystery "?" badge on the PRC flag; one stamp per spoken detail (hit + small shake + red pulse): NO AIR FORCE (a red jet streaks over, blue has none) / FEW TRUCKS / FEW RADIOS / CLOTH SHOES (frost overlay); then the blue counters march on foot by night (dotted trails) and the red giant counter cracks (boom)
paragraphs.text: The man who planned it had no air force over his troops. He had few trucks, few radios, and soldiers who crossed the mountains on foot, many in thin cloth shoes, in a bitter Korean winter. Against the most powerful military on earth.

paragraphs.tag: MAP: hook-4 | Name slam: PENG DEHUAI (real photo badge, hit + shake); three snap cuts (~3 s each, whoosh + hit): UNSAN NOVEMBER 1950 (night, bugles, ring closes on the 8th Cavalry), THE CHONGCHON NOVEMBER 1950 (blue arrows pour through the broken right flank), SEOUL JANUARY 1951 (blue arrows over the frozen Han, Seoul ring flips blue); title card PENG DEHUAI'S 3 GREATEST TACTICAL MOVES (riser + boom)
paragraphs.text: His name was Peng Dehuai. In ten weeks, he ambushed the Americans at Unsan, shattered the Eighth Army on the Chongchon River, and took Seoul. These are Peng Dehuai's three greatest tactical moves.

paragraphs.tag: ARCHIVE: Peng Dehuai portrait (PD, 3D depth); 1930s Red Army / Long March stills (licensed only); headline date card "1928 / HUNAN, CHINA"
paragraphs.text: Peng was born in eighteen ninety-eight, into a poor peasant family in Hunan province. His mother died when he was a small boy, and at times he begged for food and worked in a coal mine to survive. He became a soldier as a teenager, joined the Communists in nineteen twenty-eight, and led his men through the Long March, a year-long fighting retreat across China. Of the eighteen thousand men he set out with, about three thousand reached the end. He was blunt, stubborn and famously plain-spoken, one of the few men who would argue with Mao Zedong to his face. His soldiers called him Old Chief Peng.

paragraphs.tag: MAP: bg-1 | Korea overview (option 1, control per date): 25 JUNE 1950: red-brown North Korean arrows sweep south to the Pusan perimeter (KPA flag); 15 SEP: UN landing at Inchon (ships, arrow); the North Korean army collapses; UN arrows race north over the 38th parallel; 19 OCT: Pyongyang ring flips red (UN); UN arrows fan out toward the Yalu (China border glows); PRC flag north of the river
paragraphs.text: In June nineteen fifty, North Korea invaded the South. Within weeks, the North Koreans had pushed the Americans and South Koreans into a small corner around the port of Pusan. Then in September, General Douglas MacArthur landed behind them at Inchon. The North Korean army collapsed, and the United Nations forces, led by the Americans, crossed the Thirty-Eighth Parallel and drove north toward the Yalu River, China's border.

paragraphs.tag: MAP: bg-2 | Close on the Yalu, NIGHT 19 OCT 1950: blue PVA columns cross the river on bridges and pontoons (dotted trails); 19 OCT Pyongyang (ring) flips to UN; Peng badge (PRC flag) slides in; counter ticks ~200,000 · XIII ARMY GROUP; caption COMMANDER, CHINESE PEOPLE'S VOLUNTEERS; date card 18 OCT 1950
paragraphs.text: China had warned that it would not stand by. Mao decided to send an army into Korea. His first choice of commander turned it down, pleading ill health, so Mao gave the job to Peng. At dusk on the eighteenth of October, Peng crossed the Yalu with his leading troops. The next day, the Americans entered the North Korean capital, Pyongyang. Behind Peng, an army group of some two hundred thousand men was moving into Korea in the dark.

paragraphs.tag: MAP: move1-1 | Title card MOVE 1 · UNSAN · OCTOBER-NOVEMBER 1950. North-west Korea wide (option 1, 24 Oct control): red UN columns race north up separate valleys (ROK 6th, ROK 1st, US 1st Cavalry behind), wide gaps between them; the Taebaek mountains split Eighth Army (west) from X Corps (east), gap labelled ~50 MILES; red arrow tips reach toward the Yalu
paragraphs.text: By late October, the United Nations forces were racing for the border. They were not advancing as one solid front. They moved in separate columns, up separate valleys, with wide gaps between them, and with the mountains of the Taebaek range splitting the whole army in two.

paragraphs.tag: MAP: move1-2 | Red belief card (MacArthur badge, US 48-star): WAKE ISLAND · 15 OCT 1950: "VERY LITTLE" chance; "ONLY 50,000 TO 60,000 COULD BE GOTTEN ACROSS"; "THE GREATEST SLAUGHTER"; a red Yalu line with a tiny blue counter; red reconnaissance planes (c47g, red) sweep the mountains and see nothing
paragraphs.text: Four days before the Chinese crossed, MacArthur had met President Truman on Wake Island. Asked about Chinese intervention, he said the chances were very little. At most, he said, fifty or sixty thousand Chinese could be gotten across the Yalu, and if they tried to get down to Pyongyang, there would be the greatest slaughter. American reconnaissance planes flew over the mountains every day. They saw almost nothing.

paragraphs.tag: MAP: move1-3 | NIGHT: Peng badge. Blue columns march through the mountains by night (dotted trails, a moon icon, clock 19:00 -> 03:00; at 05:30 they vanish under camouflage (ghost outlines, snow); a red recon plane passes over (prop sound), a daytime column freezes: caption EVERY MAN STOPS IN HIS TRACKS; counters tick up: blue strength in the mountains grows
paragraphs.text: Peng saw something different. The Americans ruled the sky and the roads. So his men would use neither. A typical day's march began after dark, at seven in the evening, and ended at three in the morning. By half past five, every man, every animal and every gun had to be hidden and camouflaged. If a unit was ever caught moving by day and a plane appeared, every man had to stop in his tracks and stand still, and officers could shoot anyone who moved. Night after night, entire Chinese armies slipped into the mountains around the advancing columns, and the most powerful air force in the world never saw them.

paragraphs.tag: MAP: move1-4 | 25 OCT: ring on Unsan; first blue strike on the ROK 1st Division north of the town (impacts, MG); a prisoner icon: caption CHINESE PRISONERS; 26 OCT: a red ROK 6th Division regiment touches the Yalu at Chosan (flag pin), then blue arrows close behind it from both sides (40TH ARMY); red ROK 6th Division counters at Onjong shatter and grey (hit); ROK II CORPS ROUTED
paragraphs.text: On the twenty-fifth of October, the trap began to close. Near the town of Unsan, South Korean troops ran into fierce resistance and took their first Chinese prisoners. Further east, a South Korean regiment reached the Yalu itself, at the town of Chosan. Days later, it was cut off and destroyed, and the South Korean Sixth Division with it. The South Korean Second Corps, on the right flank of the Eighth Army, was routed.

paragraphs.tag: MAP: move1-5 | Unsan close-up (option 2: glowing fronts only), NIGHT: the Kuryong river shimmers; the US 8th Cavalry Regiment (three battalion counters) in a loose arc north and west of Unsan, gaps between them; blue PVA divisions (39TH ARMY) creep down the ridges toward the gaps; ring on the road junction south of town
paragraphs.text: The Americans sent the Eighth Cavalry Regiment of the First Cavalry Division to Unsan to steady the line. Its three battalions spread out in a wide arc north and west of the town, with gaps between them. Around them, in the hills, waited the Chinese Thirty-Ninth Army.

paragraphs.tag: MAP: move1-6 | NIGHT 1-2 NOV: bugle + whistle + horn captions (static), blue arrows pour through the gaps from three sides (MG, impacts, shake); one blue column marches over the bridge at the 3rd Battalion CP "like ROK troops", a bugle caption, then a burst of impacts on the CP (shake); a blue roadblock slams onto the road south of town (hit); stamp SURROUNDED
paragraphs.text: On the first of November, as darkness fell, the Chinese attacked. Out of the night came bugles, whistles and horns, signals for the assault, and then the infantry, not only against the front but through the gaps between the battalions. In the early hours, one Chinese column marched calmly across a bridge right up to a battalion command post. The guards let it pass, thinking the men were South Koreans. Then one of their leaders blew a bugle, and the column attacked from all sides. Behind the Americans, Chinese units set up a roadblock on the road south of Unsan.

paragraphs.tag: MAP: move1-7 | 2 NOV: two red battalion counters break out on foot over the hills, leaving guns and vehicles (greyed icons); the 3rd Battalion counter alone, ringed; red 5th Cavalry arrow pushes north toward it, stops at the blue blocking line (impacts); stamp RELIEF FAILED; 4 NOV: the ring closes, red counter greys
paragraphs.text: By dawn, two of the battalions were fighting their way out across the hills, leaving most of their vehicles and guns behind. The Third Battalion was trapped. The Fifth Cavalry tried to break through to it, lost around three hundred and fifty men, and was thrown back by Chinese troops dug in on a ridge the Americans would name Bugle Hill. At dusk on the second of November, the division commander, General Hobart Gay, made what he later called the most difficult decision of his life. He ordered the relief force to withdraw, and left the Third Battalion to its fate. It held out for two more days before the survivors tried to escape in small groups.

paragraphs.tag: MAP: move1-8 | 5-6 NOV: the blue counters fade back into the mountains (quiet), the front goes silent; red counters pull back to the Chongchon; RESULT card (Appleman): 8TH CAVALRY: OVER 1,000 MISSING AT FIRST · ~600 LOST · ROK 6TH DIVISION DESTROYED · UN ADVANCE THROWN BACK TO THE CHONGCHON; then the method card line 1: OWN THE NIGHT
paragraphs.text: At first, more than a thousand men of the Eighth Cavalry were missing. When the stragglers had found their way back, its losses still came to around six hundred men. The UN advance in the west had been thrown back to the Chongchon River. And then, on the sixth of November, the Chinese did something nobody expected. They broke contact and disappeared back into the mountains. Peng had shown what an army that owned the night could do. Own the night.

paragraphs.tag: MAP: move1-sub | Short subscribe card over the map (bell); counters idle
paragraphs.text: If you're enjoying this breakdown, consider subscribing. It really helps the channel. Now, let's move on to Peng's second great move, the trap on the Chongchon River.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 2 — BAIT THE TRAP: THE CHONGCHON AND KUNU-RI (~7:00 – ~12:00)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move2-1 | Title card MOVE 2 · THE CHONGCHON RIVER · NOVEMBER 1950. North-west Korea wide (option 1, 24 Nov control): blue counters withdraw deep into the mountains (ghost outlines); a blue arrow curls back north (LURE THEM IN); a few prisoner icons walk south to the UN lines (22 NOV: 27 PRISONERS FREED); quote card from Peng's memoir: "PURPOSELY SHOWING OURSELVES TO BE WEAK ... LURING HIM DEEP INTO OUR AREAS"
paragraphs.text: Why had the Chinese vanished? Peng had hurt the Americans, but he had not destroyed them. His men were short of food and ammunition, and the enemy was still strong. So he pulled his armies back into the mountains, and even set some American prisoners free, to make the Americans believe they faced only a small force that was already pulling out. Peng later wrote that the idea was to show themselves weak, make the enemy arrogant, and lure him deep into their areas.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 2 — BAIT THE TRAP: THE CHONGCHON AND KUNU-RI (~7:00 – ~12:00)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move2-2 | Red belief card: UN ESTIMATE ~70,000 CHINESE vs the real number ticking past it: 300,000 (ticks, hit); "12 DIVISIONS" vs 30; MacArthur badge; 24 NOV: red UN arrows start north again from the Chongchon along the valleys (I Corps west, IX Corps centre, ROK II Corps on the right flank in the mountains); the gap between Eighth Army and X Corps glows; MacArthur quote card: "SHOULD FOR ALL PRACTICAL PURPOSES END THE WAR"; small press card "HOME BY CHRISTMAS"
paragraphs.text: It worked. By late November, the UN Command believed there were about seventy thousand Chinese in Korea. In fact there were more than four times as many. On the twenty-fourth of November, the Eighth Army set off north again in what was meant to be the final offensive of the war. MacArthur flew in to see it begin, and announced that if it succeeded, it should for all practical purposes end the war. There was talk among the troops of being home by Christmas.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 2 — BAIT THE TRAP: THE CHONGCHON AND KUNU-RI (~7:00 – ~12:00)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move2-3 | Peng badge. The plan draws on: blue counters (XIII ARMY GROUP, ~200,000) in a great arc in the mountains; blue arrows on the US 2ND DIVISION in the centre (main blow); the right flank of the UN line glows: ROK II CORPS (thin red counters, ROK flags) at Tokchon; a second blue arrow aimed at it, then curling behind the American divisions toward Kunu-ri; label THE OPEN FLANK
paragraphs.text: Peng was waiting, with some two hundred thousand men of his Thirteenth Army Group hidden in the mountains ahead. His plan was to hit the whole line at once. His heaviest blows would fall on the Americans in the centre, especially the US Second Infantry Division. But on the right, out in the mountains, the flank was held by the South Korean Second Corps, the same corps his men had already broken once. If that flank gave way, his troops could swing in behind the entire American army.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 2 — BAIT THE TRAP: THE CHONGCHON AND KUNU-RI (~7:00 – ~12:00)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move2-4 | Small headline card first: 25 NOV · PENG'S HQ BOMBED (impacts on a hut icon, shake) · MAO ANYING KILLED. Then NIGHT 25 NOV: bugles, blue attacks all along the Chongchon (MG, impacts, shake) hit the US 2nd and 25th Divisions (39TH, 40TH ARMIES); at the same time two blue army arrows (38TH, 42ND ARMIES) smash into ROK II Corps at Tokchon (impacts, shake); 26 NOV NOON: red counters crack and grey; stamp RIGHT FLANK COLLAPSES
paragraphs.text: On the twenty-fifth of November, American bombers hit Peng's own headquarters. Among the dead was a young officer on his staff, Mao Anying, the eldest son of Mao Zedong. That night, the Chinese struck. Along the Chongchon River, bugles sounded in the dark and Chinese infantry hit the American divisions in the centre. Out on the right, two Chinese armies fell on the South Korean Second Corps. By noon the next day, its front had folded. The right flank of the entire Eighth Army was gone.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 2 — BAIT THE TRAP: THE CHONGCHON AND KUNU-RI (~7:00 – ~12:00)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move2-5 | 27-28 NOV: blue 38th Army pours through the hole, swinging south-west behind the American divisions toward Kunu-ri and the road south (arrows); the Turkish Brigade (red, Turkish flag) at Wawon fights a delaying battle (impacts) and is pushed back; ring on Kunu-ri; red withdrawal arrows start south; stamp ENVELOPMENT
paragraphs.text: Now Chinese troops poured through the gap and swung south-west, around the back of the American divisions, toward the crossroads at Kunu-ri and the roads leading south. A Turkish brigade sent to plug the hole fought hard, but it was pushed back. On the twenty-eighth of November, the Eighth Army began to retreat.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 2 — BAIT THE TRAP: THE CHONGCHON AND KUNU-RI (~7:00 – ~12:00)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move2-6 | Kunu-ri close-up (option 2), 30 NOV, cold dawn: the road from Kunu-ri south to Sunchon glows; blue counters (113TH DIVISION) line the ridges on both sides for ~6 MILES (bracket), a blue block at the pass (ring); a long red column of trucks, guns and men enters the valley; a side arrow: 23RD INFANTRY takes the western road via Anju (escapes)
paragraphs.text: The US Second Infantry Division had been covering the retreat, and it was one of the last to leave. Its road south ran through a narrow valley from Kunu-ri toward Sunchon. The Chinese had got there first. A Chinese division had lined the ridges on both sides of the road with machine guns and mortars, building what American historians call an elongated fire block, about six miles deep, with its heaviest fire at a pass.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 2 — BAIT THE TRAP: THE CHONGCHON AND KUNU-RI (~7:00 – ~12:00)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move2-7 | The Gauntlet: MG fire + mortar impacts rake the column from both ridges (shake), trucks burn and jam (smoke columns, red counters grey one by one); US fighter-bombers (red c47g, few, spaced) strafe the ridges (K.bombRun, shake); caption THE GAUNTLET; a counter ticks the vehicles lost
paragraphs.text: On the thirtieth of November, the division drove into it. Machine-gun and mortar fire swept the road from both sides. Trucks were hit and burned, blocking the way for the vehicles behind them, and men had to climb over the wrecks or run along the ditches under fire. American aircraft strafed the ridges again and again, but the column could only crawl forward. One regiment, the Twenty-Third Infantry, took a different road to the west and got out. For the rest, the road to Sunchon became known as the Gauntlet.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 2 — BAIT THE TRAP: THE CHONGCHON AND KUNU-RI (~7:00 – ~12:00)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move2-8 | Zoom out to all Korea (option 1, control 24 Nov -> 15 Dec cross-fade): red arrows stream south; Pyongyang ring flips blue (5 DEC); X Corps in the east pulls back to Hungnam (ships, 24 DEC); the front settles on the 38th parallel; Walker badge greyed: KILLED 23 DEC (jeep accident); result card
paragraphs.text: In the last days of November, the Second Division lost about four and a half thousand men, a third of its strength, along with sixty-four artillery pieces and hundreds of trucks. The Eighth Army fell back so fast that it lost contact with the Chinese altogether. On the morning of the fifth of December, it left Pyongyang burning behind it, and by the middle of December it was back near the Thirty-Eighth Parallel. In the east, the rest of the UN forces were evacuated by sea. And two days before Christmas, the Eighth Army's commander, General Walton Walker, was killed when his jeep collided with a truck.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 2 — BAIT THE TRAP: THE CHONGCHON AND KUNU-RI (~7:00 – ~12:00)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move2-9 | RESULT card (Mossman): US 2ND DIVISION 4,940 BATTLE CASUALTIES (15-30 NOV) · 64 GUNS LOST · PYONGYANG ABANDONED 5 DEC · EIGHTH ARMY BACK TO THE 38TH PARALLEL; method card lines 1-2: OWN THE NIGHT · BAIT THE TRAP
paragraphs.text: Peng's victory came at a cost. His soldiers had fought through a brutal winter with little food and poor clothing, and many were lost to the cold as well as to American firepower. But in a few weeks he had turned the war around. The army that had been racing for the Chinese border was now fighting to hold on to South Korea. Own the night. Bait the trap.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 3 — HIT THE SEAMS: THE THIRD PHASE AND SEOUL (~12:00 – ~16:10)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move3-1 | Title card MOVE 3 · SEOUL · JANUARY 1951. Korea overview -> 38th parallel close-up (option 1, 26 Dec control): the UN line along the Imjin and the 38th parallel north of Seoul, the Han river behind Seoul; Ridgway badge (US 48-star) slides in: NEW COMMANDER 26 DEC
paragraphs.text: Walker's replacement was General Matthew Ridgway, who arrived on the day after Christmas. He found an army that was exhausted and badly shaken, holding a line along the Thirty-Eighth Parallel just north of Seoul. Behind it lay the frozen Han River and the South Korean capital.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 3 — HIT THE SEAMS: THE THIRD PHASE AND SEOUL (~12:00 – ~16:10)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move3-2 | Peng vs Mao "duel" text cards (no likeness of Mao): 7 DEC · PENG: AT LEAST 3 MONTHS TO RECOVER vs MAO: ATTACK ACROSS THE 38TH PARALLEL; Peng's supply line drawn from the Yalu down to the parallel (dotted, flickering, bomb hits along it, K.bombRun with shake); stamp A LIMITED BLOW
paragraphs.text: Peng's own army was in trouble too. His men were worn out, short of food and winter clothing, and his supply lines now stretched hundreds of miles back to China, under constant American air attack. On the seventh of December, he told Mao his armies needed at least three months to recover. But Mao wanted another blow across the parallel, and he wanted it now. So they settled on a limited offensive: one sharp strike that a tired army could actually carry out.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 3 — HIT THE SEAMS: THE THIRD PHASE AND SEOUL (~12:00 – ~16:10)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move3-3 | Red belief card: "HOLD NORTH OF SEOUL"; close-up of the UN line (option 2): US I Corps and IX Corps divisions (big red counters, tanks, artillery) with South Korean divisions in the line between and beside them (thin red counters, ROK flags); the boundaries between them glow white; Peng badge: THE SEAMS
paragraphs.text: The UN line looked solid on the map. But the Chinese looked at who was holding each part of it. The American divisions had tanks, artillery and air support. The South Korean divisions beside them, many rebuilt after the November disaster, had far fewer heavy weapons. And they were not mixed in with the Americans, who could have backed them up. So the Chinese plan aimed squarely at the South Koreans, and above all at the two South Korean divisions holding the boundary between the two American corps north of Seoul.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 3 — HIT THE SEAMS: THE THIRD PHASE AND SEOUL (~12:00 – ~16:10)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move3-4 | NIGHT 31 DEC 1950 (New Year's Eve), snow: blue guns fire a 30-minute barrage (K.gun salvos, arcs, impacts with shake) on the ROK sectors; blue arrows cross the frozen Imjin and smash into the ROK 1st Division (impacts, MG); around midnight more arrows hit the ROK 6th; further east blue arrows hit the ROK 2nd and 5th Divisions; red ROK counters crack and stream south (hit); stamp NEW YEAR'S EVE; the US 25th Division counter beside them stays untouched (label NOT ATTACKED)
paragraphs.text: On New Year's Eve, just after dark, the Chinese guns opened fire. Half an hour later, the infantry came across the frozen Imjin River, and the heaviest blows fell exactly where the plan had aimed them: on the South Korean divisions. The American division next door was hardly touched. Around midnight, a second Chinese army struck the next South Korean division, and further east more attacks hit the South Koreans in the centre. Before dawn, the South Korean First Division had been driven out of its positions.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 3 — HIT THE SEAMS: THE THIRD PHASE AND SEOUL (~12:00 – ~16:10)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move3-5 | 1 JAN 1951: Ridgway badge drives north (jeep dotted path); trucks of retreating ROK soldiers stream past him (red counters greyed, no weapons icons); caption A BEATEN ARMY ON THE ROAD; the flanks of the US divisions now open (glow); blue arrows start curling behind them
paragraphs.text: On New Year's morning, Ridgway drove north to see for himself. He met trucks packed with South Korean soldiers heading south, with hardly a rifle among them. He jumped out of his jeep and tried to wave them to a halt, but, as one historian put it, he might as well have tried to stop the flow of the Han. With holes torn in the line, the flanks of the American divisions were open, and the Chinese were working their way around them.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 3 — HIT THE SEAMS: THE THIRD PHASE AND SEOUL (~12:00 – ~16:10)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move3-6 | 1 JAN noon: red withdrawal arrows to the Seoul bridgehead; 3 JAN 13:00: order card ABANDON SEOUL; red arrows pull back across the Han (bridges glow, then blast impacts as the UN blows them, shake), a refugee stream over the ice (grey dots, caption ~600,000 CIVILIANS LEAVE); a British rear-guard counter (UK flag) ringed and overrun (impacts); 4 JAN 1951: Seoul ring flips blue (hit); stamp SEOUL FALLS; UN line slides south to LINE D (7 JAN)
paragraphs.text: Ridgway would not let his army be trapped against the river. At noon on New Year's Day, he pulled his troops back to a bridgehead around Seoul, and on the third of January, he ordered the city abandoned. Hundreds of thousands of civilians fled south across the frozen river. The UN troops followed, blowing the bridges behind them, while a British rear guard was cut off and lost some three hundred men. On the fourth of January, the Chinese entered an empty, burning Seoul. By the seventh, the UN line had fallen back to a new position far to the south.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 3 — HIT THE SEAMS: THE THIRD PHASE AND SEOUL (~12:00 – ~16:10)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move3-7 | Blue arrows stop south of Seoul (they halt; stamp HALT · 7-8 JAN); Peng's supply line flickers back to the Yalu; card from Peng's memoir: STRENGTH "REDUCED BY NEARLY 50 PER CENT"; ghost arrow of a possible UN landing behind him (Inchon icon, dashed); zoom out
paragraphs.text: And then Peng stopped. He could have chased the retreating army further south, and many expected him to. But Peng knew his own men better. By his own account, his forces had lost nearly half their strength to battle, cold and hunger since the autumn. His supply lines were at breaking point, and he feared another American landing behind him, like Inchon. He knew the Americans had been pushed back, not beaten. So he halted his army to rest.

paragraphs.section: MOVE 3 — HIT THE SEAMS: THE THIRD PHASE AND SEOUL (~12:00 – ~16:10)
paragraphs.tag: MAP: move3-8 | RESULT card (no reliable casualty figure): SEOUL TAKEN 4 JAN 1951 · UN LINE PUSHED BACK TO LINE D · US DIVISIONS ESCAPE; method card complete: OWN THE NIGHT · BAIT THE TRAP · HIT THE SEAMS
paragraphs.text: In less than three months, Peng's armies had come from the Yalu River to south of Seoul. At Unsan, he owned the night. On the Chongchon, he baited a trap and sprang it on an open flank. And at Seoul, he hit the seams. Own the night. Bait the trap. Hit the seams.

paragraphs.tag: MAP: end-1 | Korea overview (option 1, control Jan -> Mar -> Jul 1951 -> 1953): Ridgway's counter-offensive pushes the line back north past Seoul (14 MAR 1951); blue spring offensives (APR-MAY 1951) hit and are thrown back (impacts); the line freezes near the 38th parallel: 27 JULY 1953 ARMISTICE (Peng badge signs)
paragraphs.text: His halt proved right. Within weeks, Ridgway struck back, and in March the UN retook Seoul. When Peng attacked again that spring, his men were caught in the open by American firepower and lost heavily. The war settled into a stalemate near the Thirty-Eighth Parallel, and in July nineteen fifty-three, Peng signed the armistice for China.

paragraphs.tag: ARCHIVE: Peng in the 1950s (PD); headline card "1959 / LUSHAN"; date card "1974 / BEIJING"
paragraphs.text: He came home a hero and became China's minister of defence. But in nineteen fifty-nine, he wrote Mao a private letter criticising the Great Leap Forward, as famine spread across the country. Mao turned on him, and he was purged. During the Cultural Revolution, Red Guards seized him, paraded him before rallies and beat him in interrogation after interrogation. His enemies even blamed him for the death of Mao's son in Korea. He died in custody in nineteen seventy-four, denied proper medical care. Four years later, the Party declared that the verdict against him had been wrong.

paragraphs.tag: MAP: end-2 | Korea overview: the three moves replay as rings on Unsan, the Chongchon / Kunu-ri and Seoul with their dates; Peng badge centre; method card
paragraphs.text: Peng Dehuai had no air force, few trucks and few radios. Against the most powerful military on earth, he used the night, the mountains and the enemy's own confidence. He owned the night. He baited the trap. And he hit the seams. In nineteen fifty-three, Peng said that the days had gone forever when a Western power could occupy a country in the East by setting up a few cannons on its coast. Whatever one thinks of the cause he served, on the battlefield, he had made his point.
